title: 2025-05-13 POC weekly caching sync - Nova Financial
summary: Weekly POC sync to review caching pilot results for Nova Financial's LLM-powered responses. We reviewed prefix vs KV cache hit rates, latency and token-cost savings, discussed edge cases for personalized prompts, and agreed on tuning steps (increase TTL for stable prompts, smarter hashing for personalized prefixes, additional tracing). Next: run 48-hour steady-state test, share updated benchmark sheet, and schedule a deep-dive on prompt templating with Nova's PMs.
next_steps: SE to run 48-hour steady-state cache test with TTL=300s and provide results (Liam)
Customer to provide 10 additional representative prompt templates for reuse analysis (Anika)
Redwood to share updated benchmark spreadsheet and cache tracing links (Maya)
Schedule prompt-templating workshop next week (Priya to coordinate)
SE to instrument KV-hit logging in staging for week-long run (Liam / Jae)

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-13
Time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Ortega (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood CSM), Carlos Vega (Nova ML Eng), Anika Sharma (Nova PM), Tom Reeves (Infra), Jae Kim (SRE)

Summary / Topics (auto): caching pilot, prefix vs KV, hit rates, TTL tuning, prompt reuse

[00:00] Maya: okay everyone good morning, thanks for joining the weekly caching sync. we will go over the last seven days of pilot metrics and adjust the tuning. Liam is going to walk through the numbers.

[00:18] Liam: hey team, quick preface — these are staging numbers with the workload shape you provided, ~65% short chat requests, 35% multi-turn. baseline without caching we observed avg token latency 210ms and mean cost per response X. with the current prefix + KV config we measured combined hit rate about 46%.

[00:40] Carlos: 46%? that seems promising, can you break down prefix vs KV?

[00:47] Liam: yeah prefix cache hit was 31% and KV-only hits contributed another 15% of requests. note there is overlap — some requests hit both. the effective unique requests served from cache were about 42% of total, accounting for overlap and false positives in our current hashing.

[01:12] Tom: quick question, when you say prefix cache, that's matching the first N tokens of the prompt? how are we handling variable slots?

[01:21] Liam: right, prefix cache is matching on the canonicalized prompt prefix. currently we canonicalize by template and slot placeholders for stable prompts; but per the templates you provided there is some variability we aren't capturing — especially user names and numeric ids — so we ended up with lower prefix reuse. the KV cache stores model KV cache state from prior partial sequences which helps multi-turn reuse.

[01:45] Anika: can you remind us of the TTL settings currently?

[01:49] Liam: TTL is 120 seconds for prefix keys and 60s for KV entries in staging. we used conservative defaults to avoid staleness during the initial pilot.

[02:05] Jae: what's the p95 latency with those hit rates? our SLA target is p95 < 300ms for the hosted flow.

[02:12] Liam: p95 overall is right now 420ms because of the cold tail and a set of long-running generative prompts. for cached hits p95 drops to ~180-210ms. so cache-heavy routes are well under SLA, but misses skew the overall distribution.

[02:36] Carlos: oh that gap is bigger than I'd like. where are the misses coming from — are we getting hash collisions or is it the template mismatch?

[02:43] Liam: mostly template mismatch and variable noise — things like timestamps embedded into prompts, ephemeral ids. also some requests use slightly different system instructions which prevents a prefix match. we saw about 8% hits that failed due to whitespace/formatting differences.

[03:05] Maya: that aligns with what we saw on other pilots — normalization and templating increases prefix reuse a lot. we can recommend two immediate levers: 1) increase prefix TTL to 300s for stable conversational flows; 2) add more aggressive canonicalization rules for numeric identifiers and timestamps.

[03:26] Anika: would increasing TTL cause stale responses? some prompts depend on recent state.

[03:31] Liam: good point. TTL increase is safe for the majority of prompts that are idempotent or stateless; for stateful prompts we can tag keys with a session id so they avoid long TTLs. also we can use dynamic TTLs based on prompt category detected by simple heuristics.

[03:51] Tom: any idea of cost savings from the 46% hit rate? token-level savings?

[03:57] Liam: ballpark, the pilot shows ~37% reduction in token generation volume leading to roughly 28% lower model compute spend for the test workload. this varies by prompt length — longer generation benefits more.

[04:12] Carlos: can you share a chart of hit rate vs cost?

[04:16] Liam: yes, we'll attach the benchmark spreadsheet — it's linked in the follow-up email. quick note: the KV cache gives disproportionate latency wins for multi-turn: we saw up to 2.4x speedup on sequences that reused KV entries.

[04:33] Anika: we have a lot of personalization — customer name, account # — how do you recommend handling that so we still get prefix reuse?

[04:39] Liam: two patterns: template-level placeholders (replace account numbers with <acct_id>) and using ephemeral personalization tokens that are appended to the prompt but excluded from cache key computation. Redwood supports excluding token ranges from the cache key for exactly this reason.

[05:00] Jae: is excluding parts of the prompt from a cache key supported in your private deployment as well? we need this in VPC for production.

[05:05] Maya: yes, same feature across Hosted/Dedicated/Private. we keep the API consistent; the config is per-model route.

[05:14] Carlos: can you explain the current hashing scheme and why we saw collision-like behavior?

[05:18] Liam: it's a two-part key: (route id + canonicalized prefix hash + normalized instruction block). collisions in practice are rare, but if canonicalization is noisy you get effectively different keys for the same intent. we also saw a small number of false positives due to newline differences; we already added an extra normalization pass that strips common formatting.

[05:42] Anika: what about fallback behavior — if a KV hit is partial or inconsistent, do you fall back to model?

[05:47] Liam: yes we have a graceful fallback. KV reuse is validated at the attention-block level; if mismatch is detected we recompute from scratch. there's also an automatic partial decode path where we reconstruct the minimal missing tokens then resume using the cached KV to finish generation. that keeps latency bounded.

[06:06] Tom: any security concerns with storing KV state? audit / encryption?

[06:11] Maya: KV blobs are encrypted at rest using customer-managed KMS on Private deployments; hosted deployments use Redwood-managed KMS with SOC2 controls. audit logs and access controls are available — see the security docs link we'll share.

[06:25] Carlos: good. back to tuning — what if we increase TTL to 300s and canonicalize more aggressively, what bump to hit rate do you expect?

[06:32] Liam: conservative estimate +10-14% absolute on prefix reuse if canonicalization catches numeric noise; combined hit rate could reach low 60s. p95 overall should drop closer to ~320ms in that scenario, assuming miss distribution is similar.

[06:48] Anika: where did the KV expiry come from — 60s? why shorter than prefix?

[06:54] Liam: KV expiry is shorter because KV is memory-heavy; we wanted to limit memory pressure on the instance pools during the pilot. for Dedicated or Private you can bump KV retention higher if you reserve capacity.

[07:08] Jae: what's the memory delta if KV retention goes from 60s to 300s? we need to estimate GPU memory for Dedicated.

[07:14] Liam: rough rule of thumb: KV memory cost scales with number of concurrent sessions and sequence length. for your observed concurrency (~120 active sessions) and avg seq length 512, moving to 300s increases memory usage by ~22% on our prototype config. we'll produce a sizing estimate.

[07:33] Maya: action-wise we recommend two immediate experiments: 1) 48h steady-state run with TTL prefix=300s KV=180s; 2) canonicalization sweep on the 10 highest-volume templates. we'll measure hit rate delta and p95.

[07:49] Carlos: ok let's do that. also can we test excluding personalization tokens from cache keys on a small subset of traffic?

[07:55] Liam: yes, we can flag 10% of routes to use exclusion rules and compare.

[08:02] Anika: and about the prompt templates — we will collate 10 canonical templates and send them this afternoon.

[08:07] Priya: i'll coordinate the workshop to help your PMs and engineers with templating best practices — should be helpful for long-term reuse.

[08:16] Tom: any instrumentation changes you'd like from our side? more logging?

[08:20] Liam: enable KV-hit ratio logs per route at debug for the next run and export them to the shared S3 bucket. also include request-id mapping so we can trace samples. Jae ok with that?

[08:29] Jae: yes we'll enable it in staging and open the bucket.

[08:34] Maya: quick timeline recap: Liam — running 48h test by EOD Friday; Anika — send templates by Thursday; Maya — send pilot extension and pricing; Jae — enable logs and share bucket. follow-up email will include the benchmark sheet and links.

[08:52] Carlos: anything else on edge cases — what about conversation injections or user-supplied system messages?

[08:58] Liam: system messages are part of the canonicalization; we recommend normalizing or splitting system-level instructions out of the cache key if they vary frequently. for injection attempts we have rate controls and content policies but that's out of scope for caching.

[09:14] Anika: curious — do you have a dashboard view we can use to track hit rates per-route?

[09:19] Maya: yes Redwood Console exposes per-route cache hit/miss, p95, cost estimates. we'll grant you access to a read-only dashboard for the pilot metrics.

[09:27] Tom: please add our infra alias to the console access.

[09:31] Maya: will do, Priya will send invites.

[09:36] Jae: one more infra note — if we go to Dedicated we'll want autoscaling policies to consider KV memory pressure; can Redwood autoscaler consider KV usage?

[09:45] Liam: yes autoscaler can use custom metrics including KV memory usage and cache hit ratio as signals. we'll put together recommended policies.

[09:54] Maya: ok last call for questions. anything outstanding?

[09:59] Carlos: no, thanks everyone. good progress.

Meeting end notes: agreed experiments: TTL bump, canonicalization sweep, KV tracing. Follow-up artifacts to be shared: benchmark spreadsheet, security docs link, console invite, pilot extension/pricing.
